info.name: AISafe - Flight Operations Service (Distributed & P2P Tests)
info.description:
End-to-end tests of the Flight Operations Service with two replicas (8071 and 8072) and the Aircraft & Maintenance (8081) and Airports & Routes (8092) services.

Run the folders in order. Folder 0 loads reference data into the other services from docs/postman/csv-imports (run from the repository root so the CSV paths resolve). Flight dates are generated per run, so the collection can be run repeatedly against the same services.

The last folder (Manual) needs services to be stopped by hand and is not part of a normal run.

Newman: newman run flight-operations-service/docs/flight-operations-postman-collection.json --folder "0. Setup" --folder "1. Scheduling across replicas" --folder "2. Flight lifecycle" --folder "3. Inter-service endpoints" --folder "4. Reports and import" --folder "5. Assignment 2 - CQRS and AMQP"

item.name: 1. Scheduling across replicas
item.description: Flights are partitioned by aircraft: every flight of an aircraft is stored by the replica that owns it (hash of the registration over the sorted replica URLs; JA-HND belongs to instance 1). A command sent to another replica is forwarded to the owner, where a per-aircraft database lock serialises the conflict check. Listings merge the data of all replicas.

item.name: 5. Assignment 2 - CQRS and AMQP
item.description:
Needs the message broker (RabbitMQ, or the embedded broker described in COMMANDS.md) and every service started with messaging on.

Commands (POST/PATCH /api/flights) change the write model of the replica that owns the flight and publish an event on the aisafe.exchange topic exchange. Every replica has its own durable queue, so each read model (/api/v2/flights) receives the flights of the whole cluster. The read side is eventually consistent: requests that read it wait a moment first.

It also shows messaging between services: flight.completed is consumed by Aircraft & Maintenance, and the aircraft.status.changed events of that service reach this one.

5.2 Query: the flight in the read model of instance 2

exec: setTimeout(() => {}, 1500); // eventual consistency: give the broker a moment

request.description: Instance 2 never handled this flight: its read model received it through its own queue.

item.name: Manual - Fault tolerance
item.description: Not part of a normal run: each request needs a service to be stopped first, as its description says.

item.name: M.1 Instance 2 stopped: listing still answers with local data

request.description: Stop instance 2 (8072) first. Availability over consistency: the flights of instance 1 are returned with 200.

item.name: M.2 Instance 2 stopped: unknown flight answers 503, not 404

request.description: Stop instance 2 (8072) first. The flight might be on the replica that could not be asked, so "not found" would be a guess.

item.name: M.3 Aircraft service stopped: an aircraft never seen answers 503 with Retry-After

exec: // Valid dates even when folder 1 was not run.

request.description: Stop every Aircraft & Maintenance instance first (8081-8083). JA-QQQ is not in the local catalog, so each instance is tried in order before giving up.

item.name: M.5 Instance 1 stopped: scheduling an aircraft it owns answers 503

request.description: Stop instance 1 (8071) first. JA-HND belongs to instance 1; instance 2 cannot check its flights, so it refuses instead of risking two flights at once for one aircraft (consistency over availability for this rule). Reads keep working.

item.name: M.4 Aircraft service stopped: a recently seen aircraft is still scheduled (local catalog)

request.description: Stop every Aircraft & Maintenance instance first, with messaging on. The aircraft was seen less than 10 minutes ago (event or look-up), so scheduling does not depend on the Aircraft service being up: the asynchronous integration removed that temporal coupling.
